title: Tight Time-Space Lower Bounds for Collision Finding and Element Distinctness under Label Symmetry
abstract: How much memory is needed to retain the quantum speedup for collision finding? For a uniformly random function $f:[N]\to [N]$, the BHT algorithm finds a collision using $O(N^{1/3})$ queries and a quantumly accessible classical table containing $O(N^{1/3})$ input-output pairs, whereas a logarithmic-space Grover search uses $O(\sqrt N)$ queries. Determining the optimal query-space tradeoff between these extremes remains a major open problem.   We resolve this equation within the class of label-symmetric algorithms, which treat the function $f$'s output labels as interchangeable. We prove that such algorithm that makes $T$ queries, uses $S$ qubits, and finds a collision in a uniformly random function $f:[M]\to [N]$ with constant probability satisfies $$T=Ω(N^{1/3}) \qquad\text{and}\qquad T^2S=Ω(N\log N).$$ For the setting where $M=N$, these bounds are matched by a space-efficient implementation of the BHT algorithm. As a consequence of our tradeoff, any label-symmetric algorithm for the search version of Element Distinctness on $f: [n] \to [n^2]$ must satisfy $$T=Ω(n^{2/3}) \qquad\text{and}\qquad T^2S=Ω(n^2\log n),$$ matching Ambainis's quantum walk. Thus, both tradeoffs are optimal within the class of label-symmetric algorithms.   To prove these results, we develop a space-sensitive version of the compressed oracle technique. The compressed oracle records the information learned by the algorithm in an evolving superposition of databases. Using label symmetry and representation theory, we show that an algorithm using $S$ qubits can effectively retain information about only $O(S/\log N)$ collision-free database entries. Substituting this estimate into the compressed oracle technique yields the stated tradeoffs.
summary: This paper derives fundamental, optimal time-space lower bounds for quantum algorithms solving collision finding and Element Distinctness, restricted to label-symmetric algorithms. It achieves this by developing a space-sensitive compressed oracle technique combined with representation theory. The results clarify the inherent resource trade-offs for these core problems in quantum complexity theory.
main_problem: Determining the optimal time-space tradeoff for quantum algorithms solving problems like collision finding and Element Distinctness, specifically under the constraint of label symmetry.
main_result: The paper establishes lower bounds $T = \Omega(N^{1/3})$ and $T^2S = \Omega(N \log N)$ for collision finding, and $T = \Omega(n^{2/3})$ and $T^2S = \Omega(n^2 \log n)$ for Element Distinctness, showing these bounds are optimal within the label-symmetric class.
method: The proof develops a space-sensitive version of the compressed oracle technique, combining it with label symmetry and representation theory to bound the information retained by limited quantum memory.
model_or_system: The analysis is conducted within the quantum query-complexity model, focusing on quantum algorithms applied to functions $f:[M]	o [N]$ or the decision problem of injectivity.
key_observables: Query complexity ($T$), Qubit space complexity ($S$), and the size of the domain/codomain ($N$).
important_parameters: The bounds depend critically on the structure of the problem (collision finding vs. Element Distinctness) and the assumption of label symmetry.
main_assumptions: The results are proven only for the class of label-symmetric algorithms; the general case without this symmetry remains an open problem.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by first analyzing the required information storage using a space-sensitive compressed oracle technique, then applying this to derive the specific time-space tradeoffs for collision finding and Element Distinctness, concluding with the optimality proof.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, establishing fundamental lower bounds on computational resources (time vs. memory) is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum computation, which underpins many advanced quantum simulation and control techniques.
